_comment: Short 7 in docs/CONTENT.md: a family plan has a limit for each person and a limit for the household, and the family one is not the sum.
_injury: A child's broken arm, and a parent who has not been to a doctor all year. The point needs two people with very different years.
_numbers: $1,500 each, $3,000 for the family. Round, and deliberately NOT double-counted: the line says 'not six thousand' out loud, because that is the wrong answer everyone reaches for.
_accuracy: Two plan shapes exist. Embedded: each person has their own deductible and the family one is a cap on the household. Non-embedded (common on family high-deductible plans): nothing is covered until the family limit is met. The video teaches the embedded shape, then says plainly that some plans work the other way and the SBC says which — rather than leaving a viewer on the wrong kind of plan with the wrong expectation.
_depends_on: Short 4 (the January reset) defines a deductible with the bucket. This one assumes that and adds a second bucket, which is why it is later in the order.

variants.arm: Your daughter broke her arm falling off the monkey bars. You have not been to a doctor all year.

body.text: On a family plan, you each have your own deductible. Say fifteen hundred dollars.
But the household has one too, and it is not the sum of yours.
Her bills fill her bucket, and the family bucket, at the same time.
So one person having a bad year can fill the family one on their own.
And when the family bucket is full, the plan starts paying for everyone. Including you, who has not been sick once.
Some plans work the other way, and pay nothing until the family one is full. Your plan summary says which.
Check yours before you dispute. Or upload them free at UseClaimRight.com.
